prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Medical Visual Question Answering (Med-VQA) models currently rely heavily on large-scale datasets with clean, accurate annotations. However, in the medical domain, acquiring high-quality ground truth is exceptionally difficult due to the high cost of expert annotation and the significant inter-observer variability among clinicians (label noise). Existing VQA approaches—whether classification-based or generation-based—lack mechanisms to handle this noise effectively. Furthermore, standard noise-robust learning methods from computer vision are ill-suited for multi-modal tasks and fail to model "semantic noise," where mislabeling follows a plausible medical logic rather than being random. There is a critical need for a Med-VQA framework that is robust to inherent label noise while maintaining high diagnostic accuracy.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can treat the answer prediction task as a **conditional generative denoising process**. By employing a diffusion model, we can transform the selection of an answer from a discriminative task into a coarse-to-fine refinement process. We posit that the probabilistic nature of diffusion models will allow the system to better handle the uncertainty inherent in noisy medical labels. Furthermore, we believe that the training supervision itself can be dynamically "cleaned" during the learning process by using an auxiliary mechanism to correct noisy ground truth labels into refined pseudo-labels before they are used to train the primary diffusion generator.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a unified framework composed of three synergistic modules designed to filter noise and generate accurate answers.

**1. Answer Condition Generator (ACG)**
To guide the diffusion process, we need a robust representation of the input data. We will design a module that fuses multi-modal features (visual embeddings from the medical image and textual embeddings from the question). Instead of simple concatenation, we will utilize learnable candidate answer embeddings to "query" the fused features. This will produce a dense, answer-aware condition vector that encapsulates the relevant medical context required to solve the query.

**2. Noisy Label Refinement (NLR)**
To prevent the model from overfitting to incorrect training labels, we will introduce a training-only refinement module.
*   **Auxiliary Classification:** We will use the condition vector to drive a lightweight auxiliary classifier.
*   **Robust Loss & Dynamic Adjustment:** We will employ a loss function specifically designed to be tolerant of noise (combining focal and symmetric cross-entropy concepts). The predictions from this auxiliary classifier (proto-answers) will be compared against the noisy ground truth. If they disagree, we will generate a "soft" pseudo-label that blends the noisy label with the model's prediction based on confidence.
*   **Target Generation:** These refined pseudo-labels will serve as the "clean" supervision targets for the main diffusion module.

**3. Answer Diffuser (AD)**
This is the core inference engine. We will adapt the diffusion probabilistic model architecture to operate on answer label distributions rather than image pixels.
*   **The Diffusion Process:** During training, we will add Gaussian noise to the refined pseudo-labels (from the NLR module).
*   **The Denoising Process:** The model will learn to reverse this process, predicting the noise to remove at each step, conditioned on the context provided by the ACG.
*   **Inference:** At test time, the model will start with pure noise and iteratively refine it into a sharp probability distribution over the answer classes. This allows the model to explore the solution space broadly before converging on the most likely medically accurate answer.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical Novelty:** This approach represents the first application of diffusion models to the specific problem of noisy labels in Med-VQA, classifying answers via a generative, coarse-to-fine perspective.
*   **Robustness:** The method eliminates the reliance on pristine datasets, allowing Med-VQA systems to be trained on real-world clinical data where expert disagreement is common.
*   **Semantic Noise Handling:** By refining labels based on learned representations rather than random shuffling, the system is expected to specifically handle semantic ambiguity (plausible but incorrect medical answers) better than existing noise-correction baselines.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

### Datasets
We utilized two medical visual question answering datasets, divided into training, validation, and testing sets following the MMQ method.

*   **VQA-RAD:**
    *   **Content:** Radiology dataset comprising 315 images and 3,515 question-answer pairs.
    *   **Composition:** Each image corresponds to at least one QA pair.
    *   **Question Types:** 58% closed-end (e.g., Yes/No), 42% open-end.
*   **PathVQA:**
    *   **Content:** Pathology images extracted from digital resources (textbooks, online libraries).
    *   **Size:** 32,799 question-answer pairs involving 4,998 pathology images.
    *   **Question Types:** 50.2% open-end, 49.8% closed-end.

### Noise Simulation
To simulate "Noisy Medical VQA" (NM-VQA), we introduced controlled noise into the training sets. Testing sets remained clean.
*   **Semantic Noise Generation:**
    *   **Closed-end questions:** Symmetric noise applied by randomly flipping answer choices.
    *   **Open-end questions:** Utilized a pre-trained BERT model to create a semantic space of frequent answers. Original ground-truth answers were replaced by the closest noisy label within this semantic space to mimic human annotation errors.
*   **Noise Ratios Tested:** 10% Semantic Noise, 20% Semantic Noise.
*   **Comparison Noise:** 20% Random Noise (random label shuffling).

### Implementation Details
*   **Hardware:** Single Nvidia 3090Ti GPU.
*   **Architecture:**
    *   **Vision Encoder:** Swin Transformer.
    *   **Text Encoder:** BERT.
    *   **Decoder:** Transformer decoder (in baseline) or Answer Diffuser (in DiN).
*   **Training Parameters:**
    *   **Optimizer:** Adam.
    *   **Learning Rate:** Initial rate of 1e-5.
    *   **Batch Size:** 16.
    *   **Epochs:** Maximum 100.
    *   **Loss Weight ($\alpha$):** Set to 0.5.
    *   **Momentum Decay ($\tau$):** Set to 0.99.
    *   **Diffusion Steps ($T$):** 50 (determined via ablation).
*   **Inference Strategy:** Only the Answer Diffuser (AD) module was used for prediction. The Noisy Label Refinement (NLR) module was discarded during inference.

### Evaluation Metrics
Performance was assessed using accuracy scores for:
*   **Open-ended questions**
*   **Close-ended questions**
*   **Overall accuracy**

### Baselines Compared
We compared the proposed DiN framework against:
1.  **Med-VQA SOTA:** MMBERT, Q2ATransformer.
2.  **Uni-modal Label Denoising:** SimT (Noise Transition Matrix based), CoDis (Co-teaching based).
3.  **VQA Denoising:** SNLC (Designed for natural VQA).
4.  **Baseline:** Swin Transformer + BERT encoder with a standard transformer decoder (no denoising).

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Noise Characteristics (t-SNE Analysis):** We observed that semantic noise retains semantic coherence, whereas random noise does not. In the feature space (visualized via t-SNE), ground-truth labels replaced with semantic pairs remained clustered according to medical relevance, unlike random noise which generated arbitrary and meaningless associations.
*   **Comparison of Noise Types:** We observed that semantic noise presents a more challenging task than random noise. For example, the SNLC method achieved 62% accuracy with 20% random noise but dropped to 58% with 20% semantic noise.
*   **Diffusion Process:** The proposed Answer Diffuser (AD) module processes answers from a generative perspective, gradually refining a noisy label estimation into a clean label. This contrasts with classification-based methods that select from predefined categories and generation-based methods that construct answers word-by-word.
*   **Model Corrections (Training Phase):** We observed that the DiN framework successfully corrects noisy labels during training. For instance, in a training sample with the noisy label "Left temporal lobe," the model predicted the correct "Right temporal lobe." Similarly, it corrected "Low magnification" to "High magnification" despite the noisy ground truth.
*   **Inference Predictions:** On test set data without answers, the model correctly identified "T2 weighted MRI" and "Optic nerve" in complex medical imagery.
*   **Ablation - Answer Condition Generator (ACG):** Using only the encoders, classifier, and ACG resulted in limited accuracy (68.25%) due to overfitting on noisy labels. Adding the Answer Diffuser module improved this to 71.15%, indicating the ACG effectively supports the diffusion process with reliable conditions.
*   **Ablation - Time Steps:** Unlike image generation tasks that often require 1,000 steps, we observed optimal performance at $T=50$ steps. Increasing steps to 100 did not improve performance (73.87% vs 74.24% at 50 steps), likely because the task involves class probability distribution rather than pixel-level generation.
*   **Baseline Failure Modes:** NTM-based methods (SimT) failed to capture noise patterns effectively as the number of classes grew. Co-teaching methods (CoDis) added complexity with two-branch networks but were outperformed by the DiN framework, particularly in handling semantic noise.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Medical Visual Question Answering (Med-VQA) requires the integration of visual information from medical images to accurately respond to clinical inquiries. A critical, yet underexplored, bottleneck in this domain is the prevalence of noisy labels. Unlike natural image datasets, medical annotation requires specialized expertise, leading to high inter-observer variability and significant labeling inconsistencies. Current Med-VQA approaches predominantly assume clean annotations; classification-based methods struggle with low-frequency answers, while generation-based methods often hallucinate medically invalid responses. Furthermore, existing label-denoising techniques from uni-modal tasks (e.g., random label shuffling) fail to capture the "semantic noise" specific to medical contexts, where mislabeling often retains some semantic coherence rather than being purely random. We lack a unified framework capable of robustly handling multi-modal inputs under conditions of semantic label noise.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that diffusion models can bridge the gap between classification and generation in Med-VQA by treating answer prediction as a conditional denoising process. We hypothesize that by classifying answers from a generative, coarse-to-fine perspective, we can filter out noise and model the probability intervals of class labels more effectively than deterministic classifiers.

To enable this, we will develop the **DiN (Diffusion model for Med-VQA with Noisy labels)** framework. Our core hypothesis is that a diffusion-based "Answer Diffuser," conditioned on a dedicated "Answer Condition Generator" and supervised by a dynamic "Noisy Label Refinement" module, will be able to recover clean class prototypes from noisy supervision. We further posit that training on semantically simulated noise—rather than random noise—will yield a model that mimics and corrects human-like clinical errors.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will construct the DiN framework comprising three synergistic modules: the **Answer Condition Generator (ACG)**, the **Noisy Label Refinement (NLR)** module, and the **Answer Diffuser (AD)** module.

### 1. Problem Formulation and Data Representation
We define the input as a set of medical images $\mathcal{V} = \{v_i\}_{i=1}^N$ and questions $\mathcal{Q} = \{q_j\}_{j=1}^M$, with corresponding noisy answer labels $\mathcal{A} = \{a_j\}_{j=1}^M$.
For an image-question-answer pair indexed by $k$:
*   $v_k \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}$ is the input image.
*   $a_k \in \{0, 1\}^L$ is the one-hot encoded ground truth answer label (potentially noisy), where $L$ is the number of answer classes.

We will employ a Vision Encoder (e.g., Swin Transformer) to extract visual features $f_k^v$ and a Text Encoder (e.g., BERT) to extract question features $f_k^q$.

### 2. Answer Condition Generator (ACG) Module
To provide task-specific guidance to the diffusion model, we will design the ACG module. This module will function as a transformer decoder.
*   **Input:** Fused visual and question features serve as Key ($K_{ey}$) and Value ($V_{alue}$) embeddings.
*   **Query:** We will introduce learnable candidate answer embeddings initialized randomly to serve as $Q_{uery}$.
*   **Mechanism:** A self-attention mechanism will process the answer embeddings, followed by cross-attention with $K_{ey}$ and $V_{alue}$.
*   **Output:** The module produces a fused feature $f_k^f$, which is projected via a linear layer to generate the answer-aware condition $f_k^c$:
    $$ f_k^c = \mathrm{Linear}(f_k^f) $$
    This condition $f_k^c$ will be fed into both the NLR and AD modules.

### 3. Noisy Label Refinement (NLR) Module
To mitigate the impact of noisy labels during training, we will implement the NLR module. This module operates only during the training phase to generate refined pseudo-labels.

**A. Robust Focal Loss (RFL)**
First, we will process the condition $f_k^c$ through an auxiliary linear MLP classifier to obtain a proto-answer probability distribution $\hat{p}_k$. To handle class imbalance and label noise simultaneously, we define a Noise Robust Focal Loss (RFL). Let $a_k$ be the noisy observed label and $\gamma$ be a focusing hyper-parameter. The loss is formulated as:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{RFL} = - \sum_{l=1}^{L} a_k (1 - \hat{p}_k)^\gamma \log \hat{p}_k - \sum_{l=1}^{L} \hat{p}_k \log a_k $$
This combines symmetric cross-entropy with focal loss to prevent overfitting to noisy labels.

**B. Answer Adjustment (AA) Strategy**
We will generate a refined soft pseudo-label $\bar{y}_k$ to supervise the Answer Diffuser. If the proto-answer matches the noisy label, we treat it as clean. If not, we compute a weighted combination:
$$ \bar{y}_k = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} w_t \hat{p}_k + (1 - w_t) a_k, & \hat{p}_k \neq a_k \\ a_k, & \hat{p}_k = a_k \end{array} \right. $$
Here, $w_t$ is a dynamic weighting parameter based on the Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the model's confidence across the batch size $B$, updated at iteration $t$ with momentum $\tau$:
$$ w_t = \tau w_{t-1} + (1 - \tau) \frac{1}{B} \sum_{k=1}^{B} \hat{p}_k $$

### 4. Answer Diffuser (AD) Module
The AD module is the core inference engine. It models the answer prediction as a reverse diffusion process.

**Forward Process:** We gradually add Gaussian noise to the refined pseudo-label $\bar{y}$. At timestep $t$, the noisy label $\bar{y}_t$ is defined by:
$$ q(\bar{y}_t | \bar{y}, f^c) = \mathcal{N}(\bar{y}_t; \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t} \bar{y} + (1 - \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}) f^c, (1 - \bar{\alpha}_t) \mathbf{I}) $$
where $\bar{\alpha}_t$ represents the cumulative noise schedule. Note that the mean is interpolated between the pseudo-label and the condition $f^c$.

**Reverse Process (Inference):** We will train a diffusion model parameterized by $\theta$ to denoise a random distribution back to the answer distribution. The transition is modeled as:
$$ p_\theta(\bar{y}_{t-1} | \bar{y}_t, f^c) = \mathcal{N}(\bar{y}_{t-1}; \mu_\theta(\bar{y}_t, f^c, t), \sigma_t^2 \mathbf{I}) $$
The objective is to minimize the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the predicted distribution $y$ and the refined pseudo-label $\bar{y}$:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{dif} = \mathbf{MSE}(y; \bar{y}) $$

### 5. Training and Inference Strategy
The total training objective will jointly optimize the diffusion process and the refinement process:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{total} = \mathcal{L}_{dif} + \alpha \mathcal{L}_{RFL} $$
During **inference**, the NLR module will be discarded. We will initialize $\bar{y}_T$ with random Gaussian noise and use the AD module, conditioned on $f^c$ from the ACG, to iteratively refine the distribution to obtain the final prediction $\hat{y} = \arg \max_l (y_l)$.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Framework Novelty:** We will establish the first diffusion-based framework (DiN) specifically designed for Med-VQA, utilizing a generative perspective for answer classification.
2.  **Robustness Mechanism:** By introducing the Answer Condition Generator and Noisy Label Refinement modules, we expect to theoretically decouple the clean label signal from semantic noise, offering superior robustness compared to standard noise transition matrix or co-teaching methods.
3.  **Semantic Noise Benchmark:** We will formulate a new methodology for simulating "semantic noise" (using feature space similarity via BERT) rather than random flipping, creating a more realistic benchmark for evaluating medical AI reliability.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
